column2: The Airport Spur is a proposed 1.5-mile, four-lane divided freeway in southeastern Milwaukee County connecting Interstate 94 to General Mitchell Field, with Corridor #5 recommended at an estimated cost of about $12.1–14.0 million. Alternatives evaluated included a do-nothing/no-build option, upgrading Grange Avenue or College Avenue, rapid transit and exclusive bus lanes, and five alternative freeway corridors. Principal environmental impacts include relocation of nine families and two businesses, noise levels exceeding federal standards near Hamlin Garland School (mitigated by barriers and air conditioning), and air quality impacts that DNR found would not violate National Ambient Air Quality Standards. Public response was mixed: SEWRPC, FAA, AAA, and airport interests supported the Spur, while the City of Milwaukee Common Council, state legislators, environmental groups, and Citizens Against Airport Spur opposed it, and a November 1974 county-wide advisory referendum showed 57.8% in favor.

column2: The project is a 1.5-mile, four-lane divided freeway 'Airport Spur' on new location within Corridor #5, connecting Interstate Route 94 to General Mitchell Field's terminal facilities in the City of Milwaukee, with an estimated cost of about $12.1–14.0 million. It includes interchanges at I-94, the airport entrance road, the new air cargo area, and Howell Avenue, and would also reconstruct the I-94 median between Layton Avenue and the Spur connection. Modified rapid transit service is proposed over the Spur to serve passengers and employees.

Sensitive receptors include Hamlin Garland Elementary School, residences, and nearby Holler Park. The Build Alternate would displace approximately 34–45 people in 9–12 housing units and several commercial units, with 9 families and 2 businesses remaining to be relocated.

column2: Alternatives evaluated included a do-nothing alternate, a no-build option of improving local streets and arterial highways, upgrading Grange Avenue into a multi-lane highway, rapid transit service, and five alternative freeway corridor locations (#1–#5). Citizens also proposed upgrading East College Avenue, exclusive bus lanes on the existing expressway system, an airport shuttle service, and tunnel sections. Corridor #5 was ultimately recommended and approved by FHWA as offering the least disruptive connection with minimal adverse environmental impacts, while fixed rail rapid transit was deemed inferior to bus modified rapid transit.

column2: The largest impact is acquisition of right of way and relocation of nine families and two businesses, with approximately 35 acres valued at $2.5 million removed from the local tax base. Predicted 1990 noise levels would exceed the federal 70 dBA standard near Hamlin Garland School and adjacent residences without abatement, so noise barriers and air conditioning of the school are proposed, reducing interior school levels to 45 dBA. The Department of Natural Resources found no significant impact on fish or wildlife habitat and no rare or endangered species, and DNR approved the project under Indirect Source Rules, concluding it will not violate National Ambient Air Quality Standards or significantly degrade air quality.
